title: Watermarking AI outputs
summary: How LLM watermarks bias the sampling step with keyed green lists, Gumbel sampling or SynthID tournaments, how a z-test detects them, what paraphrase and emoji attacks do, and how C2PA covers images.
outcomes: Explain how a keyed green list and a logit bonus delta plant a watermark without retraining the model
Compute the z-score and false positive rate for a given text length, gamma and green count
Explain why exponential minimum sampling and two-competitor tournaments keep each token's distribution exact
Predict when a watermark fails: low-entropy text, paraphrasing, emoji attacks, and wide hash windows
Compare text watermarks with C2PA content credentials and choose how to combine them

lessons.title: Why AI text needs a planted signal

blocks.md: Suppose a teacher, a platform or a lab wants to know whether a passage came from a particular language model. There are three broad options. A **post hoc detector** is a classifier trained to tell human from machine text. A **retrieval** system stores every output the model ever produced and searches it later. A **watermark** plants a hidden statistical signal in the text while it is being generated.

Post hoc detectors rely on differences between human and machine text, and those differences shrink as models improve. Both the original LLM watermark paper (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023) and the SynthID-Text paper (Nature, 2024) point out that such detectors can have higher false positive rates for groups such as non-native English writers. Retrieval needs the provider to store and search every interaction, which raises privacy and scale concerns.

A watermark sidesteps both problems by changing the one step the provider fully controls: **sampling**. In the GPT you built, each step produces logits over the vocabulary, a softmax turns them into probabilities, and a token is drawn. A watermark replaces that random draw with a draw biased by a **secret pseudorandom rule**. Anyone holding the rule can later re-derive it from the text alone and count how often the text obeys it.

scenes.caption: Plain generation: the model turns the context into logits and the sampler draws the next token at random. Nothing about the draw can be checked later.
Watermarked generation: a keyed hash of the recent context decides which tokens the sampler should favor at this step. The model itself is unchanged and needs no retraining.
Detection needs only the text, the tokenizer, the hash rule and the key. It re-derives the favored set at every position, counts hits and runs a test. The language model is never loaded.

blocks.md: Start with the simplest version, the **hard red list** (Algorithm 1 in Kirchenbauer et al.). Take a toy vocabulary of 8 tokens. Before generating each token, hash the *previous* token, use the hash to seed a random number generator, and use that generator to split the vocabulary into a **green list** and a **red list** of equal size. Then sample only from the green list. The fraction of the vocabulary that is green is called $\gamma$; here $\gamma = 0.5$.

blocks.title: Green lists for a toy 8-token vocabulary

scenes.caption: Each row is the green list (1) and red list (0) produced by hashing that previous token. Every row has exactly 4 green tokens, so gamma = 0.5. Simplified: real vocabularies have 50,000 or more tokens.
After "the", the green tokens are the, sat, on and slept. A hard red list model that has just written "the" can never write "cat", "dog" or "mat" next.
After "cat", a different pseudorandom split applies. Because the split depends on the previous token, no word is banned everywhere, and a detector can recompute each split from the text alone.
"the" followed by "mat" is red. In "sat on the mat", the obvious last word is forbidden. This is the core weakness of the hard rule.

blocks.prompt: A human who knows nothing about the rule writes 16 tokens. Each token lands in the green list of its predecessor with probability 0.5. What is the chance that all 16 are green, as the hard-rule model's output always is?
blocks.reveal: $0.5^{16} = 1/65{,}536 \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-5}$. A human almost never produces a long all-green run by accident, so even a tweet-length passage gives strong evidence. The watermark is a statistical signal, not a hidden message: no single token proves anything, but the count over many tokens does.

blocks.md: The hard rule damages **low-entropy** text, where one continuation is nearly forced. The paper's example: "Barack" is almost always followed by "Obama", yet "Obama" may be on the red list. Code and memorized text have the same problem. The next lesson fixes this with a soft bias.
A text watermark is a keyed, pseudorandom preference applied at sampling time. Detection re-derives the preference from the text and asks whether the text agrees with it far more often than chance.

blocks.question: Why does the scheme derive each green list from the previous token instead of using one fixed green list for the whole vocabulary?
options: A fixed list would ban half the vocabulary everywhere and be easy to spot by word counts; a context-dependent list changes every position yet is recomputable from the text
It makes generation faster because the model already computes the previous token's embedding
It makes the watermark immune to paraphrasing
The detector needs the model's hidden state, which depends on the previous token
blocks.explain: With a fixed list, half the vocabulary would never appear in watermarked text, which hurts quality and is easy to detect by counting word frequencies. Seeding from the previous token gives a fresh split at every position that anyone with the rule can recompute. It does not help against paraphrasing, and detection never needs the model.

blocks.question: Which output would be hardest to watermark, whatever scheme you use?
options: A short story written from an open-ended prompt
A list of brainstormed product names
The first 50 digits of pi, written out exactly
A casual email reply
blocks.explain: A watermark can only act where the model has real choices. The digits of pi are fully determined, so the watermarked model must produce the same tokens a human would, leaving no room for a signal. Open-ended prose has high entropy and is easy to mark.

lessons.title: The soft watermark: add delta to the green logits

blocks.md: The **soft red list** rule (Algorithm 2 in Kirchenbauer et al.) keeps red tokens available but makes green tokens more likely. At step $t$ it computes the logits $l^{(t)}$, hashes the previous token to get a green list $G$ covering a fraction $\gamma$ of the vocabulary, adds a constant $\delta > 0$ to every green logit, and samples from the softmax of the modified logits.

blocks.caption: The watermarked distribution. [k in G] is 1 for green tokens and 0 for red ones. Multiplying a probability by e^delta and renormalizing is the same thing.

blocks.md: Take the toy vocabulary from the previous lesson with the context "the cat". The previous token is "cat", so the green list is {the, cat, ran, slept}. Suppose the model's logits are sat 2.0, ran 1.9, slept 1.7, on 0.2, the -0.5, mat -1.0, dog -1.5, cat -2.0. These logits are made up for illustration; the probabilities below are computed from them exactly.

blocks.title: High-entropy step: next token after "the cat"

scenes.caption: No watermark (delta = 0). Three tokens are plausible: sat 0.334, ran 0.302, slept 0.248. Green tokens hold 0.584 of the probability mass.
delta = 2 multiplies every green token's weight by e^2 = 7.39 before renormalizing. ran rises to 0.473, slept to 0.387, and sat (red) falls to 0.071. Green mass is now 0.912.
The text is still fluent: the model was nearly indifferent between sat, ran and slept, so nudging it toward the green ones costs little quality while leaving a strong trace.

blocks.prompt: Now the context is "the cat sat on the". The model is very confident: mat has logit 6.0, cat 1.0, dog 0.5 and every other token -2.0. After "the", mat is red. With delta = 2, what happens to the chance of writing mat?
blocks.reveal: Almost nothing. mat drops from 0.988 to 0.979, and green mass rises only from 0.001 to 0.010. A logit lead of 5 over every other token dwarfs a bonus of 2. The soft rule steps aside when there is one clear answer, which protects quality but means this token carries almost no watermark evidence.

blocks.title: Low-entropy step: next token after "sat on the"

scenes.caption: No watermark: mat has 0.988 of the mass. Entropy here is 0.12 bits, versus 2.13 bits in the high-entropy example.
delta = 2: mat still gets 0.979. The rule barely changes the output, so quality is preserved and almost no evidence is added.

blocks.md: The paper makes this precise with **spike entropy**, $S(p, z) = \sum_k p_k / (1 + z p_k)$, a softened count of how many tokens have meaningful probability. Theorem 4.2 lower-bounds the expected number of green tokens in a watermarked sequence of length $T$, with $\alpha = e^{\delta}$ and $S^\star$ a lower bound on the average spike entropy computed with $z = (1-\gamma)(\alpha-1)/(1+(\alpha-1)\gamma)$:

blocks.caption: More entropy (larger S*) and a larger delta both raise the expected green count. With all mass on one token, S* is at its minimum and the bound falls to gamma T, the chance level of human text.

blocks.title: Green fraction for a perfectly flat distribution

scenes.caption: If the model spreads probability evenly over many tokens, the green fraction is gamma e^delta / (1 + (e^delta - 1) gamma). With gamma = 0.25 and delta = 2 it is 0.711, against 0.25 for human text.
gamma = 0.5: delta = 2 gives 0.881 and delta = 5 gives 0.993. This is a best case; real text mixes high- and low-entropy steps, so the observed fraction is lower. Drag gamma to explore.

blocks.md: The cost is quality. In the paper's experiments with OPT-1.3B on 200-token news continuations, perplexity measured by a larger OPT-2.7B rose from 5.1 without a watermark to 6.2 at $\delta = 2, \gamma = 0.5$, and to 11.6 at $\delta = 10, \gamma = 0.5$. Using **beam search** helps: it picks whole sequences with many green tokens, which the authors describe as "ironing in" the watermark with little perplexity cost.

blocks.code:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, WatermarkingConfig

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2")

# green list fraction gamma = 0.25, logit bonus delta = 2.0 (the library defaults),
# green list seeded from 1 previous token ("lefthash")
cfg = WatermarkingConfig(greenlist_ratio=0.25, bias=2.0, seeding_scheme="lefthash", context_width=1)

inputs = tok(["Alice and Bob are"], return_tensors="pt")
out = model.generate(**inputs, watermarking_config=cfg, do_sample=True, max_new_tokens=60)
blocks.caption: Hugging Face Transformers ships this scheme as WatermarkingConfig, a logits processor that adds bias to green tokens.

blocks.md: $\delta$ trades watermark strength against quality; $\gamma$ sets how often human text hits green by chance. The detector depends only on $\gamma$ and the hash rule, never on $\delta$, so a provider can change $\delta$ per product without changing the detector.

blocks.question: A model's next-token distribution is spread evenly over many tokens. With gamma = 0.5 and delta = 2, about what fraction of its tokens will be green?
blocks.explain: e^2 = 7.39, so the fraction is 0.5 x 7.39 / (1 + 6.39 x 0.5) = 0.881. 0.73 is the answer for delta = 1, 0.50 is human text, and 1.00 would require the hard rule (infinite delta).

blocks.question: In the paper, the watermarked generations that went undetected at 200 tokens mostly had what in common?
options: They used rare words that were often red
They were generated with beam search
They used gamma = 0.25 instead of 0.5
They were near-copies of memorized human text or followed rigid templates, so the model had few real choices
blocks.explain: Low entropy is the main failure mode. Memorized passages and templated text (such as repeated date and time formats) give the model large, confident logits, and a soft bonus of 2 cannot redirect them. Beam search actually made detection stronger.

lessons.title: Detection is a z-test on the green count

blocks.md: Detection tests a **null hypothesis**: the text was written with no knowledge of the green list rule. Under the null, each token lands in its green list with probability $\gamma$, so the green count $|s|_G$ over $T$ scored tokens behaves like a Binomial$(T, \gamma)$ count with mean $\gamma T$ and variance $T\gamma(1-\gamma)$. The detector measures how many standard deviations the observed count sits above that mean.

blocks.caption: Equation 3 of Kirchenbauer et al. Flag the text if z exceeds a threshold. The one-sided p-value is the upper tail of a standard normal.

blocks.title: Scoring a 10-token sentence with the toy green lists
blocks.code:
def detect(tokens, gamma=0.5, z_thresh=4.0):
    green = 0
    T = 0
    for prev, tok in zip(tokens, tokens[1:]):
        g_list = green_list(prev, key)   # hash prev, seed RNG
        if tok in g_list:
            green += 1
        T += 1
    expected = gamma * T
    sd = (T * gamma * (1 - gamma)) ** 0.5
    z = (green - expected) / sd
    return z, z > z_thresh

text = "the cat ran on the dog slept on the mat".split()
z, flagged = detect(text)

scenes.caption: Pair (the, cat): the green list after "the" is {the, sat, on, slept}, so cat is red. T = 1, green = 0.
Pair (cat, ran): ran is green after cat. T = 2, green = 1.
Pair (the, dog): red again. After 5 pairs, 3 green, close to the 2.5 a coin flip predicts.
Last pair (the, mat): red. Over all 9 scored pairs, 6 are green.
Under the null, green ~ Binomial(9, 0.5): expected 4.5, standard deviation 1.5. z = (6 - 4.5) / 1.5 = 1.0, far below 4. Not flagged: 9 tokens cannot carry much evidence either way.
The detector returns z = 1.0 and flagged = False. Note the first token is never scored: it has no predecessor inside the text.

blocks.md:
Now a realistic size. Take $T = 200$ tokens and $\gamma = 0.25$. Under the null the expected green count is 50 with standard deviation $\sqrt{200 \times 0.25 \times 0.75} = 6.12$. To pass $z > 4$ the text needs at least $50 + 4 \times 6.12 = 74.5$, so 75 green tokens.

- 62 green gives $z = 1.96$, p = 0.025: suggestive, not conclusive.
- 80 green gives $z = 4.90$, p = $4.8 \times 10^{-7}$.
- 100 green gives $z = 8.16$, p = $1.6 \times 10^{-16}$.

blocks.title: How fast evidence grows with length

scenes.caption: z grows like the square root of T. With gamma = 0.25 and half the tokens green, z crosses 4 at T = 48 tokens.
A stronger watermark (70% green) crosses 4 after only about 15 tokens. A weaker one needs many more: at 40% green it takes 133 tokens.
With gamma = 0.5 the same margin is harder to reach: 80% green needs 44 tokens and 70% needs 100. Drag both sliders.

blocks.md: In the paper's main setting ($\gamma = 0.5$, $\delta = 2$, $T = 200$, OPT-1.3B with multinomial sampling), the threshold $z = 4$ corresponds to 128.3 green tokens. Theorem 4.2 guaranteed at least 142.2 on average; the empirical average was 159.5 ($z \approx 8.4$), and 98.4% of generations were detected. The misses came from low-entropy generations: all 375 of the 500 generations above the 25th percentile of spike entropy were detected.

A tiny false positive rate is not zero at scale. $z > 4$ means a one-sided p of $3.2 \times 10^{-5}$: scan a million human documents and expect about 32 false flags. Hugging Face's `WatermarkDetector` defaults to $z > 3$, where the rate is $1.3 \times 10^{-3}$. Pick the threshold for the cost of a false accusation.

The normal approximation is optimistic for short texts. For $T = 50$, $\gamma = 0.25$ and 25 green tokens, $z = 4.08$ and the normal tail is $2.2 \times 10^{-5}$, but the exact binomial tail is $1.2 \times 10^{-4}$, about 5.5 times larger. Use the exact binomial when T is small.

Two more details matter in practice. **Repeated n-grams** are scored identically every time they occur, so a human text that repeats a phrase whose last token happens to be green would inflate the count. The fix is to score each (previous tokens, token) pair only once. Second, a short watermarked passage pasted into a long human document gets diluted; the follow-up paper on reliability (Kirchenbauer et al., ICLR 2024) adds **WinMax**, which searches for the window with the highest z-score.

blocks.question: A 100-token text is checked with gamma = 0.5 and 65 tokens are green. What does a detector with threshold z = 4 report?
options: Flagged: 65% is far above 50%
Not flagged: z = 3.0, which corresponds to p of about 0.0013
Not flagged: z = 1.5
Flagged: z = 6.5
blocks.explain: Expected 50, standard deviation sqrt(100 x 0.25) = 5, so z = 15 / 5 = 3.0. That is unusual for human text (p = 0.00135) but below 4. If the same 65% rate held over 200 tokens, z would be 3.0 x sqrt(2) = 4.24 and the text would be flagged.

blocks.question: Your team must keep false accusations of students below 1 in 100,000 essays. Which change to the detector achieves that most directly?
options: Raise delta during generation
Raise the z threshold to about 4.3 and use exact binomial p-values for short essays
Lower gamma to 0.1
Use a larger language model for detection
blocks.explain: The false positive rate is set by the detector's threshold on the null distribution, which does not involve delta or any model. z = 4.26 gives a one-sided p of 1e-5, and exact binomial tails avoid the normal approximation's optimism on short texts. Raising delta only helps detect watermarked text.

lessons.title: Distortion-free sampling: the Gumbel trick and SynthID tournaments

blocks.md: The green list watermark changes the output distribution: with $\delta = 2$, "sat" fell from 0.334 to 0.071. A different idea keeps the distribution exactly the same and hides the signal in *which* random numbers drive the sampler. Sampling always consumes randomness; if that randomness comes from a keyed pseudorandom function of the context, someone with the key can later check whether the chosen tokens line up with it.

Scott Aaronson described such a scheme in a 2022 talk transcript, with a prototype built by OpenAI engineer Hendrik Kirchner. Kuditipudi et al. (2023) formalize it as **exponential minimum sampling**: for each vocabulary token $i$, derive a pseudorandom number $r_i \in [0,1]$ from the key and context, then output the token that minimizes $-\ln(r_i)/p_i$, which is the same as maximizing $r_i^{1/p_i}$. This is a close relative of the Gumbel-max trick, so the scheme is often called **Gumbel sampling**.

blocks.caption: Generation and the detection score used in practice. With truly uniform r, the chosen token is an exact sample from p.

blocks.title: One step of exponential minimum sampling

scenes.caption: The model's distribution over four candidates: sat 0.40, ran 0.30, slept 0.20, on 0.10 (a simplified, renormalized toy).
The keyed hash of the context gives one uniform number per token: r = 0.23, 0.71, 0.32, 0.66. Nobody without the key can predict these.
Raise each r to the power 1/p: 0.025, 0.319, 0.003, 0.016. ran wins although sat was more likely, because ran drew a high r. Its detection score term is -ln(1 - 0.71) = 1.24.

blocks.prompt: Over many contexts the r values look uniformly random. How often will this rule output sat, the token with probability 0.40?
blocks.reveal: Exactly 40% of the time. Maximizing $r_i^{1/p_i}$ over independent uniforms picks token $i$ with probability $p_i$; a simulation with 200,000 random draws gave 0.399, 0.302, 0.199, 0.100. So each token is **distortion-free**: the user sees an ordinary sample. The bias shows up only when you look at the r values, because the winner tends to be a token whose r was high.

blocks.md: Detection sums $-\ln(1 - r_{x_t})$. For human text the chosen token is independent of the r values, so each term is an Exponential(1) variable with mean 1. For the four-token distribution above, the mean term for watermarked text is about 2.0 (simulated). For a spiky distribution (0.97, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01) it is only about 1.14: the same entropy limit as before.

Distortion-free per token is not the same as diverse. Because r is a deterministic function of the key and the last few tokens, the same prompt and context always produce the same output. Kuditipudi et al. instead use a long random key sequence with a random starting offset, and detect by aligning the text against the key with an edit-distance cost. They report detection at p <= 0.01 from 35 tokens even after 40 to 50% of tokens were randomly edited (OPT-1.3B and LLaMA-7B).

**SynthID-Text** (Dathathri et al., Nature 2024) is Google DeepMind's production scheme. It has three parts: a random seed generator (a hash of the last $H = 4$ tokens and a secret key), a sampling algorithm called **Tournament sampling**, and a scoring function. The seed feeds $m$ **watermarking functions** $g_1, \dots, g_m$ that assign each token a pseudorandom g-value. The paper mainly uses Bernoulli(0.5) g-values: 0 or 1 with probability 0.5 each.

Tournament sampling draws $2^m$ candidate tokens from the model's distribution (repeats allowed), pairs them up, and in layer 1 keeps the candidate with the higher $g_1$ value, breaking ties at random. Winners are re-paired and judged by $g_2$, and so on until one token remains. The example below uses $m = 3$ and the same four-token distribution.

scenes.caption: Eight samples from p = (sat 0.4, ran 0.3, slept 0.2, on 0.1). Each adjacent pair will play one match.
Layer 1 g-values from the keyed seed: sat 0, ran 1, slept 1, on 1. on beats sat, slept beats sat, on beats sat. slept and ran tie at 1, and a coin flip picks ran.
Layer 2 uses a different function, g2: on 0, slept 1, ran 1 (green and red in the layer 1 row). slept beats on and ran beats on.
Layer 3 uses g3, where slept and ran both score 0, so a coin flip decides and slept is the output. Its g-values are 1, 1, 0: above the 0.5 average a human token would show.

blocks.prompt: Consider one layer: two candidates drawn from p, the one with g = 1 wins, ties broken by a coin. Averaged over random g-values, what is the probability that token x is the output?
blocks.reveal: Exactly $p(x)$. Both candidates are x with probability $p(x)^2$. Otherwise x is one of two different candidates with probability $2p(x)(1-p(x))$ and wins half the time (its g is independent of the opponent's), contributing $p(x)(1-p(x))$. The total is $p(x)^2 + p(x) - p(x)^2 = p(x)$. With two competitors per match the tournament is **single-token non-distortionary**; the paper proves this and notes that more than two competitors per match makes it distortionary but stronger.

blocks.caption: Expected layer-1 g-value of the output. For p = (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1) the sum of squares is 0.30, giving 0.675 instead of 0.5. A fully confident model gives 0.5: no evidence.

blocks.md: Detection computes the mean g-value over all $T$ tokens and $m$ layers, $\text{Score}(x) = \frac{1}{mT}\sum_t \sum_\ell g_\ell(x_t, r_t)$, and compares it with 0.5. The paper also describes weighted and learned Bayesian scoring functions that do better. Experiments generally use $m = 30$ layers. More layers add evidence per token, but each layer uses up some of the available entropy, so the gain diminishes.

Production results reported in the paper:

- A live Gemini experiment over about 20 million watermarked and unwatermarked responses found thumbs-up rates differing by 0.01% and thumbs-down by 0.02%, both statistically insignificant. SynthID-Text was then used to watermark Gemini and Gemini Advanced.
- On Gemma 7B-IT served on 4 TPU v5e chips, latency rose from 15.527 to 15.615 ms per token with 30-layer tournaments (0.57%), versus 0.26% for Gumbel and 0.28% for Soft Red List sampling.
- An algorithm combines watermarking with **speculative sampling**, which production systems use for speed.

blocks.code:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, SynthIDTextWatermarkingConfig

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("repo/id")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("repo/id")

cfg = SynthIDTextWatermarkingConfig(
    keys=[654, 400, 836, 123, 340, 443, 597, 160, 57],  # one key per tournament layer; keep secret
    ngram_len=5,                                        # seed from the previous 4 tokens
)
inputs = tok(["your prompt"], return_tensors="pt")
out = model.generate(**inputs, watermarking_config=cfg, do_sample=True, max_new_tokens=200)
blocks.caption: Open-source release in Hugging Face Transformers (v4.46.0 onward). The blog recommends 20 to 30 random keys and ngram_len 5; detection uses a Bayesian detector you train on your own watermarked and unwatermarked outputs.

blocks.md: Green lists shift probabilities toward a keyed subset (distortionary). Gumbel sampling and two-competitor tournaments keep each token's distribution exact and hide the signal in correlations between chosen tokens and keyed random values. All of them need entropy to work.

blocks.question: A SynthID-style tournament is run with 3 candidates per match instead of 2, to strengthen the watermark. What changes?
options: Nothing: any tournament preserves the model's distribution
The watermark gets weaker because ties are more common
Detection now requires running the language model
The watermark gets stronger but the output distribution is no longer exactly the model's, so quality can drop
blocks.explain: The paper proves two competitors per match is single-token non-distortionary and that more competitors make tournament sampling distortionary, with a stronger watermark. That is SynthID's distortionary configuration. Detection still only needs the key and the g-functions.

blocks.question: A watermarked model answers "What is 17 x 3?" with "51". Why will SynthID's mean g-value for this answer be close to 0.5?
options: The tournament only runs on outputs longer than 200 tokens
The model is almost certain of each token, so all candidates in the tournament are the same token and every match is decided by a coin flip
Numbers are excluded from the vocabulary hash
g-values are reset at the start of each response
blocks.explain: When p is concentrated on one token, all 2^m candidates are that token, so the output is fixed regardless of the g-values. The output's g-values are then just the token's pseudorandom values, averaging 0.5. Factual, low-entropy answers carry little watermark.

lessons.title: Attacks, limits, and content credentials for images

blocks.md: A watermark has to survive a user who wants to remove it. Kirchenbauer et al. group attacks into **insertions**, **deletions** and **substitutions** of tokens. Because each green list depends on the previous token, a single edit can hurt twice: the edited token may be red, and the token after it now gets a different, freshly randomized green list.

The cleverest attacks make the model do the work. In the **emoji attack** (credited to Riley Goodside), the user asks the model to put an emoji after every word, then deletes the emojis. Each real word's green list was seeded by an emoji, so after deletion every word is rescored against a list seeded by a different predecessor.

blocks.title: The emoji attack on a 1-token-context watermark

scenes.caption: The model was asked to write an emoji (E) after every word. It generated with the watermark on, so each word was chosen to be green given the E before it.

The user deletes every E. The detector now scores cat given the, ran given cat, and so on: pairs that never appeared during generation. Each word is green only by chance, with probability gamma, and z falls to around 0.

blocks.md: Other surface tricks include **homoglyphs** (Cyrillic letters that look Latin), zero-width characters, and edits that change how neighboring words tokenize. The paper's defense is to normalize text before hashing. Generative attacks like the emoji trick can be discouraged by training the model to refuse them, but they remain the strongest attacks the authors list.

**Paraphrasing** is the most practical attack. Krishna et al. (2023) built DIPPER, an 11B-parameter paraphraser. On GPT2-XL generations it cut watermark detection from 100% to 57.2% at a 1% false positive rate, and DetectGPT from 70.3% to 4.6%. They still found watermarking the most resilient of the detectors they attacked. Kirchenbauer et al. measured an automated attack that swaps words using T5-Large:

blocks.title: Detection AUC under a T5 word replacement attack

scenes.caption: Detection AUC as the attacker replaces a growing fraction of words: 0.998, 0.988, 0.954, 0.838, 0.696. Replacing 10% barely matters.
The price: perplexity of the attacked text rises from 6.3 (no attack) to 13.1, 21.2, 28.4 and 33.9. Scrubbing the watermark with a weaker model visibly degrades the text.

blocks.md: Paraphrases also leak. In the ICLR 2024 reliability study, even strong human paraphrases of watermarked text were detected after about 800 tokens on average at a $10^{-5}$ false positive rate, because rewrites keep n-grams of the original. When 150 watermarked tokens were pasted into a 600-token human passage, detection AUC stayed above 0.95.

The context width $h$ (how many previous tokens seed the green list) is a tradeoff. With $h = 1$ an attacker can learn many red lists by querying a detector; brute force needs about $|V|^{1+h}$ queries. But with $h = 5$, one edited token re-randomizes 5 downstream lists, adding about 2.5 red tokens in expectation at $\gamma = 0.5$ (**attack amplification**). The paper suggests $h = 2$ or 3, or its self-hash variant.

Watermarks have structural limits too. Sadasivan et al. (2023) show **recursive paraphrasing** can sharply lower detection, and that an attacker can infer the hidden signature well enough to **spoof** it, making human text look watermarked. The SynthID paper lists stealing, spoofing and scrubbing as open problems. A watermark only covers providers who apply it, and open-weight models can be run with it switched off. A missing watermark never proves a human wrote the text.

blocks.question: A provider uses a green list seeded by the previous 5 tokens (h = 5, gamma = 0.5). An attacker edits 1 token in the middle of a long text. Roughly how many extra red tokens does that one edit create, in expectation?
blocks.explain: The edited token changes the seed for the next 5 positions, and each of those tokens is then green only by chance (probability 0.5), so about 2.5 extra red tokens. That is what the paper calls attack amplification, and why a small h or the self-hash scheme is suggested.

blocks.md: Images use different tools. **Tree-Ring** watermarks (Wen et al., 2023) plant a pattern in the Fourier transform of a diffusion model's initial noise; the detector inverts the diffusion process to recover the noise and checks for the pattern, which is designed to survive crops, flips and rotations. Separately, **C2PA Content Credentials** attach signed provenance metadata instead of hiding a signal.

In the C2PA specification, a **manifest** holds **assertions** (for example an action `c2pa.created` with the IPTC digital source type `trainedAlgorithmicMedia` for generative AI output). The assertions go into a **claim** that the signer signs with an X.509 certificate, and a **hard binding** (a cryptographic hash) ties the manifest to the exact bytes of the asset. Manifests are stored in JUMBF boxes inside JPEG, PNG, MP4 and other formats. A **soft binding**, either a fingerprint or an invisible watermark, lets a validator find the manifest again in a repository when the embedded copy is stripped or the file is re-encoded.

blocks.title: Content credentials through an upload that strips metadata

scenes.caption: The tool builds a manifest saying the image was created by a generative model, hashes the image bytes (hard binding), signs the claim, and embeds the manifest in the file. It also registers the manifest under a soft binding.
The image is uploaded. Like many pipelines, the platform re-encodes it and drops the embedded metadata, so the manifest no longer travels with the file.

The validator finds no embedded manifest but reads the invisible watermark, looks up the matching manifest, and checks its signature against trusted certificates. Simplified: the spec also covers time-stamps, revocation and ingredient checks.

blocks.md: Watermarks are statistical evidence woven into content; content credentials are signed claims attached to a file. Metadata is easy to strip but cryptographically strong; watermarks survive some edits but can be scrubbed, spoofed or never applied. Real deployments combine them.

blocks.question: A news site wants to show readers whether a photo came from a generative model. Which combination best matches what each tool can and cannot do?
options: Use only an invisible watermark: it proves who made the image and cannot be removed
Use only C2PA metadata: the hard binding hash survives re-encoding
Use C2PA for signed, detailed provenance, plus a watermark as a soft binding to recover the manifest when metadata is stripped, and treat a missing signal as unknown rather than human-made
Run a post hoc AI-image classifier instead, since it needs no cooperation from the generator
blocks.explain: A hard binding hash breaks when bytes change, which is why C2PA defines soft bindings. Watermarks can be scrubbed or spoofed and say little on their own. Post hoc classifiers lack calibrated false positive guarantees. Absence of any signal is not evidence of human authorship.
